sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Given that [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n \times n] symmetric matrix over [MATH: \mathbb{R}], the spectral theorem states the following:

  • The eigenvalues of [MATH: A] are all real.

  • Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

  • [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are real.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable. Hence, it is diagonalizable.

  • Statement III is false. According to the theorem, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal, but two eigenvectors corresponding to the same eigenvalue may not be orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Content:
We can write an [MATH: n\times n] symmetric matrix [MATH: A] in terms of a sum of products of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Content:
Specifically, if [MATH: \mathbf{u}_i] denotes an orthonormal eigenvector of [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_i] for [MATH: i=1,\ldots, n], then

Content:
[MATH: A=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T.]

Content:
Expressing a symmetric matrix [MATH: A] in this way is called the spectral decomposition of [MATH: A.]

Content:
To demonstrate, let's find the spectral decomposition of the [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [− 3|3; 3|5]]

Content:
The eigenvalues of [MATH: A] are [MATH: \lambda_1 = 6] and [MATH: \lambda_2 = -4,] and the corresponding eigenvectors are

Content:
[MATH: [1; 3]]

Content:
The spectral decomposition of [MATH: A] is given by

Content:
[MATH: A =\sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1 \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2 \mathbf u_2^T,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf u_1] and [MATH: \mathbf u_2] are orthonormal eigenvectors of [MATH: A] corresponding to [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2,] respectively.

Content:
First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

Content:
[MATH: u_{1}|= (v_{1})/(‖v_{1}‖) = (1)/(sqrt(10))[1; 3]; u_{2}|= (v_{2})/(‖v_{2}‖) = (1)/(sqrt(10))[3; − 1]]

Content:
Therefore, the spectral decomposition of [MATH: A] is

Content:
[MATH: A|= λ_{1}u_{1}u_{1}^{T} + λ_{2}u_{2}u_{2}^{T}; = 6 ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(10))[1; 3] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(10))[1|3] + (− 4) ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(10))[3; − 1] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(10))[3|− 1]; = 6 ⋅ (1)/(10)[1; 3] ⋅ [1|3] + (− 4) ⋅ (1)/(10)[3; − 1] ⋅ [3|− 1]; = 6_(⏟)_(λ_{1}) ⋅ [(1)/(10)|(3)/(10); (3)/(10)|(9)/(10)]_(⏟)_(u_{1}u_{1}^{T}) + (− 4)_(⏟)_(λ_{2}) ⋅ [(9)/(10)|− (3)/(10); − (3)/(10)|(1)/(10)]_(⏟)_(u_{2}u_{2}^{T}).]

Content:
In this decomposition, the matrix [MATH: \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T] is the orthogonal projection matrix that maps any [MATH: \mathbf x \in \mathbb R^2] onto the subspace spanned by [MATH: \mathbf u_i.]

The spectral decomposition of a [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix [MATH: A] is given by

[MATH: A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T,] where [MATH: \mathbf u_1] and [MATH: \mathbf u_2] are orthonormal eigenvectors of [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2,] respectively.

First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

[MATH: u_{1}|= (v_{1})/(‖v_{1}‖) = (1)/(sqrt(13))[2; 3]; u_{2}|= (v_{2})/(‖v_{2}‖) = (1)/(sqrt(13))[− 3; 2]]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: A|= λ_{1}u_{1}u_{1}^{T} + λ_{2}u_{2}u_{2}^{T}; = 6 ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(13))[2; 3] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(13))[2|3] + (− 7) ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(13))[− 3; 2] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(13))[− 3|2]; = 6 ⋅ (1)/(13)[2; 3][2|3] + (− 7) ⋅ (1)/(13)[− 3; 2][− 3|2]; = (1)/(13)(6 ⋅ [2; 3][2|3] + (− 7) ⋅ [− 3; 2][− 3|2]); = (1)/(13)(6 ⋅ [4|6; 6|9] + (− 7) ⋅ [9|− 6; − 6|4]); = (1)/(13)[− 39|78; 78|26]; = [− 3|6; 6|2].]

[MATH: A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T,]
where [MATH: \mathbf u_1] and [MATH: \mathbf u_2] are orthonormal eigenvectors of [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2,] respectively.

Therefore, we have

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The spectral decomposition of a [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix [MATH: A] is given by

[MATH: A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T,] where [MATH: \mathbf u_1] and [MATH: \mathbf u_2] are orthonormal eigenvectors of [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2,] respectively.

Moreover, [MATH: \mathbf u_i\cdot \mathbf u_i^T] is the projection matrix corresponding to [MATH: \mathbf u_i.]

First, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to [MATH: \lambda=-1.] Computing [MATH: A-(-1)I,] we get

[MATH: A − (− 1)I|= [3|− 2; − 2|0] − (− 1)[1|0; 0|1] = [4|− 2; − 2|1].]

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix [MATH: M] which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [4|− 2|0; − 2|1|0]|R_{2}|:=R_{2} + (1)/(2)R_{1}; ∼[4|− 2|0; 0|0|0]]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). Thus, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain [MATH: x_1=\dfrac12x_2.] Hence, the general solution is

[MATH: [(1)/(2)x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Therefore, setting [MATH: x_2=2,] we get the eigenvector

[MATH: [1; 2]]

where [MATH: \| \mathbf{v} \| = \sqrt{5}.] Dividing [MATH: \mathbf{v}] by its norm, we obtain the normalized eigenvector:

[MATH: [1; 2]]

Finally, the required orthogonal projection matrix is given by

[MATH: u ⋅ u^{T}|= (1)/(sqrt(5))[1; 2] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(5))[1|2]; = (1)/(5)[1; 2] ⋅ [1|2]; = (1)/(5)[1|2; 2|4].]

[MATH: A = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1\cdot \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2\cdot \mathbf u_2^T,]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n\times n] symmetric matrix over [MATH: \mathbb{R}.] The spectral theorem states the following:

Content:
- The eigenvalues of [MATH: A] are all real.
- The eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.
- The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue equals the multiplicity of that eigenvalue as a root of the characteristic polynomial.
- [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying True Statements Regarding the Spectral Theorem

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: A] is a real symmetric matrix, which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: A] must have all real eigenvalues
2. [MATH: A] is diagonalizable
3. If [MATH: \mathbf{u}] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}] are two eigenvectors, then [MATH: \mathbf{u} \perp \mathbf{v}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given that [MATH: A] is an [MATH: n \times n] symmetric matrix over [MATH: \mathbb{R}], the spectral theorem states the following:

- The eigenvalues of [MATH: A] are all real.
- Eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.
- [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix are real.
- Statement II is true. Indeed, any symmetric matrix with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable. Hence, it is diagonalizable.
- Statement III is false. According to the theorem, eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues must be orthogonal, but two eigenvectors corresponding to the same eigenvalue may not be orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

---

Item 3 — Question 1

1. [MATH: A] must have [MATH: 5] distinct eigenvalues
2. [MATH: A] is orthogonally diagonalizable
3. If [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] are two eigenvectors that correspond to the same eigenvalue, then [MATH: u⊥v]

Choices:
a. I and III only
b. II only
c. I only
d. II and III only
e. I and II only

Item 5 — Tutorial: The Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix

Content:
We can write an [MATH: n\times n] symmetric matrix [MATH: A] in terms of a sum of products of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

Content:
Specifically, if [MATH: \mathbf{u}_i] denotes an orthonormal eigenvector of [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_i] for [MATH: i=1,\ldots, n], then

Content:
[MATH: A=\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T.]

Content:
Expressing a symmetric matrix [MATH: A] in this way is called the spectral decomposition of [MATH: A.]

Content:
To demonstrate, let's find the spectral decomposition of the [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix [MATH: A,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [− 3|3; 3|5]]

Content:
The eigenvalues of [MATH: A] are [MATH: \lambda_1 = 6] and [MATH: \lambda_2 = -4,] and the corresponding eigenvectors are

Content:
[MATH: [1; 3]]

Content:
The spectral decomposition of [MATH: A] is given by

Content:
[MATH: A =\sum_{i=1}^2 \lambda_i \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T = \lambda_1 \mathbf u_1 \mathbf u_1^T + \lambda_2 \mathbf u_2 \mathbf u_2^T,]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf u_1] and [MATH: \mathbf u_2] are orthonormal eigenvectors of [MATH: A] corresponding to [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2,] respectively.

Content:
First, let's normalize our eigenvectors:

Content:
[MATH: u_{1}|= (v_{1})/(‖v_{1}‖) = (1)/(sqrt(10))[1; 3]; u_{2}|= (v_{2})/(‖v_{2}‖) = (1)/(sqrt(10))[3; − 1]]

Content:
Therefore, the spectral decomposition of [MATH: A] is

Content:
[MATH: A|= λ_{1}u_{1}u_{1}^{T} + λ_{2}u_{2}u_{2}^{T}; = 6 ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(10))[1; 3] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(10))[1|3] + (− 4) ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(10))[3; − 1] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(10))[3|− 1]; = 6 ⋅ (1)/(10)[1; 3] ⋅ [1|3] + (− 4) ⋅ (1)/(10)[3; − 1] ⋅ [3|− 1]; = 6_(⏟)_(λ_{1}) ⋅ [(1)/(10)|(3)/(10); (3)/(10)|(9)/(10)]_(⏟)_(u_{1}u_{1}^{T}) + (− 4)_(⏟)_(λ_{2}) ⋅ [(9)/(10)|− (3)/(10); − (3)/(10)|(1)/(10)]_(⏟)_(u_{2}u_{2}^{T}).]

Content:
In this decomposition, the matrix [MATH: \mathbf{u}_i \mathbf{u}_i^T] is the orthogonal projection matrix that maps any [MATH: \mathbf x \in \mathbb R^2] onto the subspace spanned by [MATH: \mathbf u_i.]

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Spectral Decomposition of a Symmetric Matrix

Example Prompt:
Suppose that

[MATH: \qquad] [MATH: [2; 3]] and [MATH: [− 3; 2]]

are eigenvectors of a [MATH: 2 \times 2] symmetric matrix [MATH: A] that correspond to the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1=6] and [MATH: \lambda_2=-7,] respectively. Find the matrix [MATH: A.]

The spectral decomposition of a [MATH: 2\times 2] symmetric matrix [MATH: A] is given by

where [MATH: \mathbf u_1] and [MATH: \mathbf u_2] are orthonormal eigenvectors of [MATH: A] corresponding to the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2,] respectively.

[MATH: u_{1}|= (v_{1})/(‖v_{1}‖) = (1)/(sqrt(13))[2; 3]; u_{2}|= (v_{2})/(‖v_{2}‖) = (1)/(sqrt(13))[− 3; 2]]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: A|= λ_{1}u_{1}u_{1}^{T} + λ_{2}u_{2}u_{2}^{T}; = 6 ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(13))[2; 3] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(13))[2|3] + (− 7) ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(13))[− 3; 2] ⋅ (1)/(sqrt(13))[− 3|2]; = 6 ⋅ (1)/(13)[2; 3][2|3] + (− 7) ⋅ (1)/(13)[− 3; 2][− 3|2]; = (1)/(13)(6 ⋅ [2; 3][2|3] + (− 7) ⋅ [− 3; 2][− 3|2]); = (1)/(13)(6 ⋅ [4|6; 6|9] + (− 7) ⋅ [9|− 6; − 6|4]); = (1)/(13)[− 39|78; 78|26]; = [− 3|6; 6|2].]
